title: Gersonides invented the Jacob's staff to measure the height of stars, and the Pope asked for its translation into Latin

trailer.text: Levi ben Gerson, Gersonides, was a medieval Jewish philosopher, and according to the Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers he is perhaps best known for his invention of the Jacob's staff.
He lived in Orange, a town that in his time was not part of France.
His instrument was a long rod with a sliding plate, and it was used to measure the heights of stars above the horizon.
The material on the instrument was translated into Latin during his lifetime, at the request of Pope Clement VI.
One of the craters of the Moon, 'Rabbi Levi', is named after him.

stations.title: A man who wrote almost nothing about himself

paragraphs.text: According to the Biographical Encyclopedia, Levi ben Gerson wrote almost nothing about himself, and his contemporaries also wrote little about him.
According to MacTutor, little is known of his life, and what one historian states as certain is sometimes disputed by another.
According to the Encyclopedia, apart from several trips to Avignon he most likely spent his entire life in Orange.
According to MacTutor, he almost certainly married the sister of Judah Delesfils, and no record of children from the marriage has survived.
There is no evidence of where he studied the sciences, and so, according to MacTutor, many experts believe he was self-taught in them.
According to MacTutor, the common theory is that he made a living from his knowledge of medicine.
According to the Encyclopedia, there is evidence that he may have followed the traditional occupation of his family, moneylending.
According to MacTutor, the King of France, Philip the Fair, expelled the Jews from France in 1306 and seized their property, but Levi was not affected.
In Provence, too, Jews had a difficult time.
In the preface to 'The Wars of the Lord', Levi wrote that their suffering was so intense that it prevented thought and reflection.
According to the Encyclopedia, the popes in Avignon had a lenient policy toward the Jews.
In this period the creative life of the Jews flourished, particularly in philosophy and theology.

stations.title: A book twelve years in the making

paragraphs.text: In 1317 he began writing an essay on the problem of creation, from which 'The Wars of the Lord' later grew.
The work took twelve years.
In the astronomical part, in 136 chapters, he critically reviews the astronomical theories of his time.
He also compiles astronomical tables and describes one of his inventions.
According to the Encyclopedia, what distinguished him from the Jewish philosophers before him was a deep command of mathematics and a belief that good instruments yield accurate observations.
According to MacTutor, he wanted accurate instruments in order to make sure that any theoretical model agreed with what is seen in the sky.
More than once he preferred his own observations to those of Ptolemy, and said so explicitly.
According to MacTutor, Levi invented the Jacob's staff, an instrument for measuring the angular distance between celestial objects.
He himself called it 'Megalleh Amukot', and his Christian contemporaries called it Bacullus Jacobi, Jacob's staff.
According to the Encyclopedia, the instrument was used to measure the heights of stars above the horizon.
It was a long rod with a sliding plate, with which the distance between stars could be found.
According to MacTutor, six or seven perforated tablets slid along the staff.
Each tablet was an integral fraction of the staff's length, to facilitate calculation.
According to the Encyclopedia, he suggested several refinements to the astrolabe.
According to MacTutor, he designed a transversal scale for reading fifteenths of a degree (1/15 degree) on the graduated outer circle of the astrolabe.
He observed the Moon, the Sun and the planets using a camera obscura, and also eclipses.
After observing a solar eclipse in 1337, he proposed a new theory of the Sun and tested it by further observations.
He criticized Ptolemy's model and built a model of his own: solid spheres separated by layers of fluid.
According to MacTutor, his lunar model dispensed with epicycles and agreed with observation much better than Ptolemy's model.
According to MacTutor, rejecting the Ptolemaic system, a widely accepted model of the universe, showed courage.
He also briefly discussed a model with the Sun at the center, and rejected it in favor of the Earth at the center.
According to the encyclopedia, chapter 99 of the fifth book contains astronomical tables commissioned by several Christian clerics.
According to MacTutor, the tables were made for the meridian of Orange in 1320.

stations.title: The Pope asks for a translation

paragraphs.text: The material on the instrument, in chapters 4–11 of the astronomical part of 'The Wars of the Lord', was translated into Latin at the request of Pope Clement VI.
This happened during his lifetime.
According to MacTutor, the translation includes later revisions made by Levi himself.
Levi dedicated one of his works to Pope Clement VI.
According to the Encyclopedia, his works were known to his contemporaries, both Jewish and Christian.
Isaac de Lattes wrote of him, in the preface to one of his books, that he was the author of many valuable works.
The astronomy chapters were omitted from the first printed edition of 'The Wars of the Lord'.
They have survived in four manuscripts.
One of the craters of the Moon, 'Rabbi Levi', is named after him.
According to MacTutor, in his work 'Maaseh Hoshev' he used induction, and it is one of the earliest texts to do so.
In a work on sines he proved the sine theorem for plane triangles, but he was not the first to present it.
According to the Stanford Encyclopedia, he is the first Jewish philosopher to use the analytic, scholastic method.
His commentary on the Book of Job, completed in 1325, was one of his most popular works.
According to MacTutor, only in recent years has he received his rightful place in the history of philosophy.

stations.title: What did not succeed, and what caused controversy

paragraphs.text: According to MacTutor, his method for constructing the scale of the Jacob's staff is theoretically correct, but requires extremely difficult measurements.
So perhaps it was never put into practice.
According to MacTutor, some of his beliefs were far from the truth, for example what he thought about the Milky Way.
According to the Encyclopedia, he was an avid supporter of astrology, and it played an important role in his views on free will and providence.

He began writing a prediction on the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter, possibly at the request of Pope Clement VI, and the work was completed by his Latin translator, Peter of Alexander, and his brother, Solomon.
Levi died in 1344, a year before the conjunction he predicted for March 1345.
According to the Encyclopedia, the Black Death, which arrived in Europe in 1347, was provided by the prediction with numerous astrological credentials.
In 1348 the medical faculty of the University of Paris reported on the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter, which was seen as bringing death and disaster.
According to MacTutor, his scientific work was often in conflict with Judaism.
In the preface to 'The Wars of the Lord' he wrote that the Law cannot prevent us from considering to be true that which our reason leads us to believe.
According to the Stanford Encyclopedia, one of his opponents called his book 'Wars against the Lord'.
He was quoted a great deal, even if sometimes only to be criticized.
According to MacTutor, his philosophical work was rejected, whereas his commentaries occupied a central place in Jewish theology.
